decisions.name: HandMaintainedVersionString
decisions.what: appVersion is a hand-edited Text constant rather than read from cabal-generated Paths_pelotero_engine.version
why: Reading from Paths_* requires plumbing the autogen module into the import graph and pulls Data.Version handling into every site that logs the version.
The risk is drift: bumping the .cabal version without bumping this constant produces a binary that lies about itself in the fetch log.
Mitigation is process: a release checklist item, not a code-level guarantee.

appName: compile-time constant; canonical application name used in logging and any place that needs to identify this binary as the producer of a record
OverloadedStrings is enabled solely so the string literal types as Text without explicit pack
appVersion: hand-maintained version string; not derived from cabal's PackageInfo_pelotero_engine, so it can drift from the .cabal file unless updated by hand
intended to be embedded wherever the engine identifies itself (audit fields, future fetch-log enrichment)

decisions.name: PureKernelSplitFromEffects
decisions.what: scorePlayerPure / sumBattingPoints / sumPitchingPoints / rowToBattingStats / rowToPitchingStats are pure and exported separately from the effectful scoreLeague / scoreTeam
why: The pure kernel is the part hedgehog tests can hit without spinning up Postgres.
Splitting them lets us unit-test 'given these rows, the score is X' without an in-memory effect runner — just a record literal and a function call.

The pure functions deliberately take and return DB row types (BattingRow / PitchingRow), not domain types, because the round-trip BattingRow -> BattingStats -> Points loses no information; storing-then-loading and direct-scoring agree by construction.

decisions.name: MissingLeagueReturnsNothing
decisions.what: scoreLeague and scoreTeam both return Maybe; Nothing means the league config (or the team) wasn't in the DB
why: Distinguishes 'this league doesn't exist' from 'this league has zero teams' (Just LeagueScore { lscTeams = [] }).
An empty lineup still produces a TeamScore with zero points — dropping such teams would be a presentation choice the caller should make.
Doesn't validate that the team belongs to the league in scoreTeam — caller's responsibility to check.

decisions.name: InningsPitchedRoundTripsViaText
decisions.what: rowToPitchingStats reconstructs pitInningsPitched as Text via renderInningsPitched, even though the DB stores exact outs
why: scorePitching's contract is 'consume PitchingStats whose pitInningsPitched is the wire-format string', and we honour that contract regardless of whether the input came from a live wire response or a DB round-trip.

The round-trip parseInningsPitched . renderInningsPitched is exact for valid outs (precondition: the DB column is constrained to non-negative outs, which it is by virtue of the conversion at write time in Pelotero.Sync.Boxscores.inningsPitchedOuts).

Pitting both pitInningsPitched and pitOuts means scorePitching has redundant inputs; today it prefers parseInningsPitched, but if a future caller sets pitOuts only, the round-trip would silently zero them out. Note for future refactor.

decisions.name: PeriodFromUtcStartEnd
decisions.what: scoreLeague derives lscPeriodStart / lscPeriodEnd by utctDay'ing lcScoringStart and lcScoringEnd from the league config
why: league_config stores UTCTime instants because lineup-lock cutoffs are timezone-sensitive (see Pelotero.Domain.League decision ScoringPeriodAsUtcTime), but the DB game.game_date is Day, so the query needs Day bounds.
Truncating UTCTime to Day in UTC is correct only because game_date is also stored in UTC at write time. A change to either column's timezone semantics would break this silently.
The two utctDay calls happen once per scoreLeague invocation; not a perf concern.

decisions.name: PerGamePerStatTypeReadsAreNplusM
decisions.what: buildPlayerMaps issues one getBattingForGame and one getPitchingForGame per game in the period, then buckets by player
why: Simple to reason about; each call is a single index hit on (game_id) and the result is a few dozen rows.
For a one-week period across one league: ~100 games × 2 calls = 200 transactions. For a season: ~2400 games × 2 = 4800 transactions. Acceptable but not great.
Replacement: a single SELECT joining game.game_date with game_player_batting / game_player_pitching, returning rows directly bucketed by player_id. Worth doing if scoring becomes a hot path.

rowToBattingStats: mechanical Int32 → Int widening on every Maybe field; lossless
rowToPitchingStats: Int32 → Int widening on every Maybe field
pitInningsPitched is reconstructed via renderInningsPitched <$> pitchingInningsPitchedOuts; pitOuts is preserved from the row directly so callers that prefer it still get an exact value
sumBattingPoints: sumPoints over (scoreBatting m . rowToBattingStats) — a fold; empty list yields zeroPoints
scorePlayerPure: produces a PlayerScore with batting + pitching subtotals and their sum
pure: same inputs → same output, no IO or randomness
the canonical hedgehog target for scoring property tests (when those exist)

scoreLeague.intent: Score every team in a league across the league's configured scoring period
notes: returns Nothing if the league config row is absent
empty lineups produce zero-point TeamScores rather than being dropped
uses the team's CURRENT lineup_slot rows against historical boxscores — see openIssues

scoreTeam: scores a single team using the league's period
returns Nothing if either the league config or the team is absent
does NOT validate that the team belongs to the league
buildPlayerMaps: fetches all games in [startDay, endDay] then partitions batting and pitching rows by player
buildBattingMap: Map.insertWith (++) per row; per-player order within the resulting list is reverse insertion order
scoreOneTeam: uses LS.getSlotsForTeam (current lineup), not a historical snapshot
lookupAndScore: Map.findWithDefault [] for both rows; a player on the lineup with no boxscore activity scores zero

openIssues.name: CurrentLineupAgainstHistoricalBoxscores
openIssues.what: scoreLeague applies the team's CURRENT lineup_slot rows to every game in the scoring period, not the lineup that was active on the day each game was played
why: Real fantasy leagues lock lineups daily — Tuesday's lineup scores Tuesday's games, Wednesday's lineup scores Wednesday's games.
If an owner moves a player between lineup slots mid-period, every prior day's score retroactively changes when re-computed.
Owners notice this and lose trust in the system. This is a correctness bug, not a missing feature.
Fix requires either a lineup_slot_history table (every change recorded with timestamps) or per-game lineup snapshots written at game start.
blocking: any production use that retains scoring history across lineup edits

openIssues.name: NplusMQueriesAtScale
openIssues.what: buildPlayerMaps issues 2 transactions per game in the period
why: Acceptable today (~200 transactions per weekly score for one league).
At full season × multiple leagues this becomes a real cost.
Replace with a JOIN-driven query when scoring becomes a hot path.

decisions.name: TeamsBeforePlayersOrdering
decisions.what: syncRosters upserts all teams first, builds a TeamId -> DbTeamId map, then upserts players using that map to resolve playerRowCurrentTeamId
why: Players carry a foreign key to team via current_team_id; if the team doesn't exist in the DB at insert time, the FK either fails (with constraint enforcement) or installs a dangling reference (without).
Building the map in memory between the two phases avoids a second round-trip per player to look up the DB team id.
The two phases share one syncedAt timestamp from the Clock effect, so last_synced_at on team and player rows match exactly for a given sync run, useful when reasoning about staleness.

decisions.name: ProviderAgnosticEntryPoint
decisions.what: syncRosters takes already-converted [Team] and [Player] domain values plus a precomputed SHA-256, never touches wire types or HTTP
why: Keeps the sync pipeline testable in isolation: tests construct domain values directly and run against in-memory effect interpreters.
Allows alternative providers (a future non-MLB feed, manual data import) to reuse this exact code path by doing their own wire->domain conversion upstream.
The SHA is computed by the caller because only the caller has the raw bytes; passing it in here keeps this module from depending on Crypto.Hash.

decisions.name: ResourceLiteralActiveRosters
decisions.what: syncRosters writes fetchLogResource = 'active-rosters' as a literal rather than parameterising it
why: The MLB roster endpoint queried (rosterUrl) filters to activeStatus=ACTIVE on the server side, so this resource name is the literal truth of what was fetched.
If a future scope adds inactive/40-man/minor-league fetches, that becomes a new resource name passed in by the caller, not a flag here.

syncRosters.intent: Provider-agnostic upsert pipeline: teams, then players, then fetch-log entry, returning a small summary
notes: single Clock.now call shared by both team and player upserts; both rows get identical last_synced_at
fetchLogResource hardcoded to 'active-rosters'; scope is supplied by the caller (typically the season as Text)
fetchLogRecordCount is the player count, NOT the team count; teams are bookkeeping
fetchLogId and fetchLogFetchedAt are Nothing on the inbound row; the DB layer fills them via DEFAULT
syncTeamsUpserted / syncPlayersUpserted are simply length of the input lists, not a count of how many rows actually changed (an upsert that hit an existing row still counts)
consumes: CLI sync command (process startup or scheduled run)

upsertAllTeams: produces Map TeamId DbTeamId where the key is the upstream MLB id and the value is the surrogate DB id, in the order traverse visits the input list
extId is the show-of-Int rendering of unTeamId; the DB stores it as Text per the team_external_id schema
teamRowId is Nothing on insert; the DB layer assigns the surrogate id
upsertAllPlayers: uses the team map from upsertAllTeams to resolve playerRowCurrentTeamId; players whose upstream team isn't in the map (unknown / minor league call-up) get Nothing for current_team_id
extId mirrors the upsertAllTeams convention: show-of-Int from unPlayerId
discards the DbPlayerId returned by upsertPlayerByExternalId; the caller doesn't need it (sync pipeline writes player rows but doesn't link them further here)
handToChar takes T.head of renderHandedness ('L', 'R', 'S'); the DB schema stores handedness as a single character per legacy convention

openIssues.name: IdempotencyByChecksumNotWired
openIssues.what: syncRosters always upserts every team and player; it computes the payload SHA, writes it to provider_fetch_log, but never reads the prior value to skip
why: The original refactor plan called for re-running sync to be a no-op when the upstream checksum hasn't changed.
The shortcut is one getLastFetch call before doing work: if the previous fetch's payload_sha256 matches the new one, return early with zeros.
Currently the cost is ~700 player upserts + 30 team upserts on every CLI invocation, even when nothing changed.

Fix is small: getLastFetch provider 'active-rosters' scope; compare fetchLogPayloadSha256 to the inbound payloadSha; bail with SyncResult { syncTeamsUpserted = 0, syncPlayersUpserted = 0, syncFetchSha256 = payloadSha } if equal.

openIssues.name: ExternalIdEncodingIsImplicitContract
openIssues.what: T.pack . show . unTeamId in upsertAllTeams must agree byte-for-byte with the same encoding in Pelotero.Sync.Schedule.resolveTeam, but the contract lives in source comments rather than the type system
why: If anyone changes either encoding without changing the other, every game upsert silently skips because resolveTeam returns Nothing for every team.
Same shape of bug as the legacy 'commissioner' vs 'comissioner' JSON-key bug: an implicit string contract crossing module boundaries.
Fix: a single `externalIdFromTeamId :: TeamId -> Text` helper exported from a shared module (Pelotero.Domain.Id or a new Pelotero.Provider.ExternalId), used by both sites.
Same problem applies to PlayerId (Sync.Players + Sync.Boxscores) and GameId (Sync.Schedule + Sync.Boxscores).

openIssues.name: HandednessCharRoundTripPartial
openIssues.what: handToChar = T.head . renderHandedness; T.head is partial
why: renderHandedness today returns one of 'L' / 'R' / 'S', all length 1, so T.head never throws — the safety lives in the renderHandedness exhaustive sum, not in the type.
If a future Handedness constructor renders to an empty Text or a multi-character string, this silently misbehaves (truncates) or throws.
The DB column for bat_side / pitch_hand is Text, not CHAR(1) — there's no actual storage advantage to encoding as Char first.

Fix: either store Text end-to-end (delete handToChar, change PlayerRow's batSide / pitchHand fields to Maybe Text), or expose a total handChar :: Handedness -> Char from Pelotero.Domain.Player so the Char path is type-safe.

decisions.name: PerGameFetchLogEntry
decisions.what: syncBoxscores writes one FetchLogRow per game (resource = 'boxscore', scope = the GameId as text), not one row per batch
why: Catch-up runs ('which boxscores are new since last sync?') become a single getLastFetch query per gameId, which is the natural primitive for incremental work.
A per-batch row would force the caller to remember which games it included, defeating the purpose of an external log.
Cost: high write volume on a fresh-season backfill (~2400 rows for a full season). Acceptable; provider_fetch_log is append-only and not a query hot path.

decisions.name: MissingPlayerSilentSkip
decisions.what: If lookupPlayerByExternalId returns Nothing for a boxscore entry's playerId, the entry is silently skipped (no upsert, no warning, no error)
why: Real cause: roster sync hasn't run for that player yet (mid-season callup, traded mid-game). Re-running after the next roster sync recovers the data.
Failing the whole game would lose 25 known-good batting lines because of one unknown player.
Trade-off: silently skipping means no operator visibility. A future improvement would be to count skipped entries in BoxscoreSyncResult so the operator can detect when this is happening at scale.

decisions.name: MissingTeamSilentDegradation
decisions.what: If a boxscore entry has a TeamId that isn't in the local DB, the team_id field is set to NULL rather than skipping the entry
why: The batting/pitching row is still useful without team attribution (player's stats are intact); team is a join convenience.
MLB occasionally ships parentTeamId values for teams that haven't been ingested (international roster expansions, mid-season ownership swaps).
Symmetrical to player handling above but lossier — at least the player would re-sync; an unknown team_id never gets backfilled. Worth flagging if it becomes common.

decisions.name: InningsPitchedOutsConversionAtWriteTime
decisions.what: inningsPitchedOuts prefers parseInningsPitched . pitInningsPitched over the wire's pitOuts field
why: MLB's pitOuts and pitInningsPitched can disagree (rare; usually only during live-update windows). The IP string is the canonical source of truth.
Falls back to pitOuts only if the IP string is absent or unparseable.
Returns Nothing if both are absent — preserves the 'didn't pitch' signal rather than fabricating a 0.

syncBoxscores.intent: Process a list of upstream GameIds: resolve each to DbGameId, fetch raw boxscore bytes, decode, convert, and upsert per-player batting and pitching rows
notes: iterates input order; no concurrency at this layer
accumulates per-game results into a BoxscoreSyncResult so partial failures don't abort the batch
boxConvertWarnings is concatenated across all successfully-processed games

syncOne: GameNotKnown: lookupGameByExternalId returned Nothing; caller must run schedule sync first
FetchFailed: HTTP or transport-level failure from MLBClient
ParseFailed: Aeson decode failure on the raw bytes
writes FetchLog after a successful upsert pass, NOT before — a partial-write scenario doesn't get logged as a successful fetch
upsertEntries: missing player → skip entry (counts unchanged); missing team → degrade team_id to NULL
boxBatting Nothing → no batting row written; boxPitching Nothing → no pitching row written
battingRowFor: mechanical Maybe Int → Maybe Int32 widening for every stat field
pitchingRowFor: same as battingRowFor; innings pitched goes through inningsPitchedOuts
inningsPitchedOuts: prefers parsed pitInningsPitched over wire pitOuts when both present
falls back to pitOuts on parse failure or absent IP string
returns Nothing iff both are absent
sha256Hex: raw ByteString → hex-encoded Text via SHA-256

decisions.name: SkipGamesWithUnknownTeams
decisions.what: syncSchedule resolves both away and home teams via lookupTeamByExternalId; if either is missing, the entire game is skipped and counted in schedGamesSkipped
why: The schedule endpoint can include teams that haven't been ingested yet (spring training affiliates, all-star game rosters, exhibition opponents).
Inserting a game with a NULL or fabricated team_id violates the foreign-key contract and silently corrupts later joins.
Skipping is recoverable: re-run after a roster sync and the game shows up. Failing the whole batch on one missing reference is not.
The skip count is surfaced in ScheduleSyncResult so operators can detect when this is happening at scale.

decisions.name: FetchLogResourceLiteralSchedule
decisions.what: syncSchedule writes fetchLogResource = 'schedule' as a literal rather than parameterising it
why: Mirrors the convention in Pelotero.Sync.Players where 'active-rosters' is the literal resource name.
If a future scope adds e.g. minor-league schedule fetches, that becomes a new resource string, not a flag here.

syncSchedule.intent: Provider-agnostic upsert pipeline for already-converted [Game] domain values
notes: writes one fetch-log row per call with resource = 'schedule', scope supplied by caller (typically a date-range string like '2025-04-01..2025-04-07')
fetchLogRecordCount is the total games count, NOT just upserted games; matches the input list length so an operator can compare against schedGamesUpserted to detect skip-rate
single Clock.now call shared across all game upserts in this run
iteration order is the input list order; not stable across runs because the upstream wire conversion preserves API order

upsertOneGame: returns True on successful upsert, False on skip (either team unresolved)
extId is show-of-Int from unGameId, matching the convention in Pelotero.Sync.Players
discards the DbGameId returned by upsertGameByExternalId; downstream boxscore upserts re-resolve via lookupGameByExternalId at scoring time
resolveTeam: wraps lookupTeamByExternalId, converting TeamId -> Text -> Maybe DbTeamId
the show-of-Int convention here MUST match upsertAllTeams in Pelotero.Sync.Players or every game gets skipped
implicit cross-module contract: anywhere a TeamId becomes an external id Text, the encoding is exactly T.pack . show . unTeamId

openIssues.name: IdempotencyByChecksumNotWired
openIssues.what: syncSchedule always upserts every game even when the payload SHA matches the previous fetch
why: Same gap as Pelotero.Sync.Players.IdempotencyByChecksumNotWired.
Schedule sync is heavier than roster sync (more rows, more team-resolution work), so the win from short-circuiting is bigger.
Fix: same shape — getLastFetch provider 'schedule' scope; compare SHAs; bail if equal.

openIssues.name: ExternalIdEncodingIsImplicitContract
openIssues.what: resolveTeam encodes TeamId as T.pack . show . unTeamId; must match upsertAllTeams in Pelotero.Sync.Players exactly
why: See Pelotero.Sync.Players.ExternalIdEncodingIsImplicitContract — same gap, this is the consumer side.
The source comment on resolveTeam already calls this out: 'the show-of-Int convention here MUST match upsertAllTeams in Pelotero.Sync.Players or every game gets skipped.'
A comment in source isn't a contract; the type system is. Fix is a shared helper.

decisions.name: UrlsIsolatedAsSwapPoint
decisions.what: All MLB Stats API URLs live in this single module with no other logic; the only way to talk to the upstream service is via this module's exports
why: If MLB changes the API base or moves an endpoint, this is the only file that needs editing.
If a future provider replaces MLB entirely, this module is the natural delete-and-rewrite boundary.
Side effect: discourages ad-hoc URL construction scattered through fetch code.

rosterUrl: pre-filters to activeStatus=ACTIVE on the server side; inactive players are not returned
uses /sports/1/players (sport id 1 = MLB), not /people, because /people requires explicit ID lists
teamsUrl: uses sportId=1 (MLB) only; minor-league teams are not returned
scheduleUrl: language=en is hardcoded; the MLB API supports other locales but the engine doesn't model them
startDate and endDate are passed as raw String; caller is responsible for the YYYY-MM-DD format MLB expects
scheduleDateUrl: convenience wrapper for single-day queries; the MLB API does not have a separate per-day endpoint, so we issue a range query with start==end
boxscoreUrl: v1 endpoint; returns the boxscore object whose shape is parsed by Pelotero.MLB.Wire.Boxscore
gameStatusUrl: v1.1 endpoint (note the version difference from boxscoreUrl); /feed/live carries scheduled-vs-final status that the boxscore endpoint does not surface cleanly
currently UNUSED in the sync pipeline; reserved for the future 'is this game final yet?' check before scoring. Effectively dead code at present.

decisions.name: WarningsBesideValuesNotInsteadOf
decisions.what: Conversion functions return ([ConvertWarning], Maybe a) or ([ConvertWarning], a) so warnings accumulate without halting the batch
why: MLB ships partial records during spring training; halting on the first one means losing the other 700 valid players.
Treating malformed records as exceptions would conflate parse errors (caught upstream by Aeson) with data-quality warnings (this layer's job).
The caller decides whether to log warnings, ignore them, or fail loudly.

decisions.name: MLBLooseDateFormat
decisions.what: parseDate uses '%Y-%-m-%-d' instead of '%Y-%m-%d'
why: MLB's schedule endpoint occasionally returns dates without zero-padding ('2024-3-5' instead of '2024-03-05').
The %-m / %-d directives accept both padded and unpadded forms.
Strict %m/%d would silently drop ~5% of pre-season games.

decisions.name: InvalidPlayerIdDropsRecord
decisions.what: convertPlayer drops players with id <= 0 entirely (returns Nothing) and emits an InvalidPlayerId warning
why: An id of 0 or negative is structurally meaningless; the surrogate-key lookup would fail and the rest of the row would be junk anyway.
Position and handedness warnings, in contrast, downgrade to Nothing for that field while keeping the rest of the player; the player is still useful as a name + team reference.
An invalid id removes the only stable identity the record has, so there is nothing left worth keeping.

decisions.name: BoxscoreNeverWarns
decisions.what: convertBoxscore returns an empty warning list, even though the wire shape has many optional fields
why: Boxscore stats are EXPECTED to be partial (a position player has no pitching stats, and vice versa).
Treating absence as a warning would flood the logs.
Genuine boxscore parse errors are caught upstream by Aeson.
If invariant warnings (e.g. negative counts) become useful, this is the place to add them.

decisions.name: DateParseFailureSilentlyDropsEntireDate
decisions.what: convertDateEntry returns ([], []) on date parse failure without emitting an InvalidGameDate warning
why: InvalidGameDate is a defined ConvertWarning constructor but no current code path produces one — it exists for the rendering pass and as an extension point.
Real MLB dates parse via the loose-padding format; failure here would indicate a structural feed change, not a data-quality issue worth surfacing per game.
Known gap: a date corruption in one entry silently loses an entire day's games. Documented as a known limitation.

renderWarning: renders each ConvertWarning constructor as a single line of stable text
format is conventional: 'convert: <subject> <id> <verb> <detail>'; downstream log scrapers can rely on the leading 'convert: ' prefix
tshow uses Show on the int id, so player ids appear without quotes
logWarnings: writes each warning as a separate stderr line; suppresses output entirely when the list is empty (Control.Monad.unless on null)
logWarnings = logWarningsTo stderr; the Handle-parameterised version exists but is not exported
logWarningsTo: private helper; targets a specific Handle. Currently only stderr is used in production but the indirection is what makes warning behaviour testable
convertPlayer: returns ([InvalidPlayerId], Nothing) for ids <= 0; the empty-warning case never produces Nothing here
useName / useLastName / nameSlug all default to T.empty when absent (orEmpty); the DB schema requires NOT NULL, so empty is the safe default
playerActive is non-optional in the wire shape; if MLB ever drops it, parsing breaks at Aeson level, not here
currentTeam is decoded as Maybe; teamless players (free agents, just-released) get Nothing for playerTeamId
convertPlayers: concats per-player warnings; the resulting list is in input order (well-defined because the envelope's player list is a list)
uses mapMaybe to filter out the Nothing cases (invalid ids); does NOT preserve a placeholder for them

notes: tries abbreviation first, then code; if both are present and one parses while the other is unknown, prefers the parsed one without warning (intentional: MLB sometimes ships an obsolete code with a current abbreviation)
if NEITHER parses but at least one is present, emits UnknownPosition with the abbreviation if available else the code
if both are Nothing, returns ([], Nothing) silently — the position field is genuinely optional for some records (managers/coaches mistakenly returned in the people endpoint)

convertHand: WireHandRef wraps a Maybe Text; this function handles WireHandRef Nothing (silent), WireHandRef (Just code) parseable (silent), and WireHandRef (Just code) unknown (warning)
no validation that batSide and pitchHand are consistent for switch-hitters; they are independent fields
convertSchedule: folds over wseDates building (warnings, games) in date order; warnings are reversed relative to date entry order due to the foldr accumulation pattern (newWs <> ws)
produces GameSchedule wrapping a flat [Game]; the per-date grouping in the wire format is discarded
off-days and missing date entries simply produce no games and no warnings
convertDateEntry: if the date string fails parseDate the WHOLE date entry is dropped silently — see decision DateParseFailureSilentlyDropsEntireDate
wdeGames Nothing means 'no games scheduled'; treated as []
delegates per-game conversion to convertGame which then attaches its own warnings
convertGame: extracts away/home team ids from the wire's nested teams.away.team.id and teams.home.team.id
if either is missing, emits MissingTeamRef with the gamePk and returns Nothing for the game
preserves the gameDate by carrying the parsed Day in from convertDateEntry
parseDate: returns Nothing for any unparseable input; never throws
uses %-m/%-d for MLB's loose padding (see decision MLBLooseDateFormat)
convertBoxscore: returns ([], entries) — never emits warnings (see decision BoxscoreNeverWarns)
concatenates away-side then home-side entries; team identification on each entry uses wbpParentTeamId from the wire, NOT the away/home position
the GameId comes from the caller (Convert doesn't see the URL the boxscore was fetched from)
boxsideEntries: iterates Map.elems of the players map; the wire keys ('ID660271') are discarded — the player id inside the value is authoritative
missing batting or pitching stats default to emptyBatting / emptyPitching; the scoring layer must NOT scale those zeroes (handled by respecting Maybe Int)
convertBatting: mechanical field-by-field copy from WireBoxBatting to BattingStats; no derivation, parsing, or fallback
any divergence between the two record shapes is a compile error here
convertPitching: same mechanical copy as convertBatting; pitInningsPitched preserves the wire's Text representation ('6.2'), NOT a parsed out count — see Pelotero.Domain.Stats.parseInningsPitched
orEmpty: Maybe Text -> Text helper, falling back to T.empty
used to avoid scattering 'fromMaybe T.empty' through the conversion code
tshow: used in renderWarning to embed numeric ids in messages

decisions.name: WireToDomainTeamPrivate
decisions.what: wireToDomainTeam is not exported; it is duplicated by hand in Pelotero.Effects.MLBClient
why: Exporting it would create a circular concern: Fetch shouldn't be a public utility module, it's the production HTTP path.
The conversion is one record literal with four fields; duplicating it is cheaper than the import discipline of having both Fetch and MLBClient depend on a shared private module.
If a third caller appears, this should move to a Convert-level helper.

decisions.name: PayloadShaIsTeamsBytesThenPlayersBytes
decisions.what: computeSha hashes the concatenation of teamsBody (raw bytes) followed by playersBody (raw bytes), in that order
why: Order matters for stability: if a future fetch reorders the calls, a re-fetch with identical content would produce a different SHA, breaking change-detection.
Using the lazy-then-strict transform inside fetchRosters is a one-place implementation detail and not part of the SHA's semantics.
Teams-then-players matches the order they're parsed and converted in the same function.

fetchRosters.intent: Real-HTTP roster fetcher: pulls teams and players, parses both, converts to domain, returns FetchedRosters with payload SHA
notes: two HTTP calls happen sequentially, not concurrently; latency is teams + players, not max(teams, players)
if either fetch errors at HTTP level, returns Left with the URL in the message
if either body fails to parse (Aeson), returns Left with 'Teams parse failure: ...' or 'Players parse failure: ...' prefix
warnings from convertPlayers are surfaced in frWarnings; team conversion does not produce warnings (mechanical record build)
frPayloadSha is over the concatenation of raw response bodies (see decision PayloadShaIsTeamsBytesThenPlayersBytes)

wireToDomainTeam: wtLocationName is Maybe Text in the wire; defaults to T.empty (NOT 'Nothing' lifted somewhere) because Team.teamLocationName is non-Maybe

fetchSchedule.intent: Real-HTTP schedule fetcher for a date range
notes: single HTTP call; parses through Pelotero.MLB.Wire.Schedule then converts via Convert.convertSchedule
warnings are passed through as fsWarnings
returns Left on HTTP error or parse failure

fetchBoxscoreRaw: returns the raw response body as ByteString without parsing
the caller (typically a stat-collection loop) parses with Pelotero.MLB.Wire.Boxscore + Pelotero.MLB.Convert.convertBoxscore at the point of use
this asymmetry vs. fetchRosters/fetchSchedule is deliberate: boxscore fetches are sometimes archived raw before processing
fetchUrl: private helper; one HTTP GET, returns the body or an HTTP error message
uses Network.HTTP.Simple.httpLBS so request setup is implicit in parseRequest
non-2xx responses are returned as Left, not thrown
computeSha: SHA-256 of the input bytes, hex-encoded as Text
uses Crypto.Hash.SHA256; matches what Aeson's strict decode sees byte-for-byte

decisions.name: FlatRecordPerStatsCategory
decisions.what: The batting and pitching wire records list every Maybe Int field individually rather than using a Map Text Int
why: Named fields make the conversion to BattingStats / PitchingStats a mechanical record-to-record copy that the compiler verifies.
A Map-based representation would defer typo-detection to runtime: a missing key would silently be Nothing instead of failing at compile time when added to BattingStats.
The cost is verbose Aeson FromJSON instances, but those are write-once.

decisions.name: InningsPitchedAsText
decisions.what: wbpInningsPitched is decoded as Maybe Text rather than Maybe Double
why: MLB sends '6.2' meaning six and two-thirds innings; decoding as Double gives 6.2 the floating-point number, which is wrong by 6.667 - 6.2 = 0.467.
Keeping it as Text propagates the raw string to the scoring layer where Pelotero.Domain.Stats.parseInningsPitched converts it to an exact out count.
This is a known historical bug in legacy fantasy systems; preserving the string is the simplest defense.

decisions.name: ModuleLevelFieldNotes
decisions.what: Field-level meaning notes for this wire module (chase has no signatures here, only data + instances)
why: wbsTeams is the only top-level field of WireBoxscore; the boxscore JSON has many more (ratings, officials, info), all deliberately ignored.
WireBoxTeams.wbtAway / wbtHome are required Aeson fields (.: not .:?) — a boxscore without both sides is a parse failure.
WireBoxTeam.wbtPlayers is Map Text WireBoxPlayer keyed by 'ID<playerId>' strings (e.g. 'ID660271'); the prefix is ignored at the converter (the playerId inside the value is authoritative).
WireBoxPlayer.wbpPersonId is the only stable identity; wbpFullName is preserved for debugging but unused in conversion.
WireBoxPlayer.wbpParentTeamId is nullable to accommodate occasional MLB feed glitches; if missing, BoxscoreEntry.boxTeamId is Nothing and the entry is harder to join later.
WireBoxPlayer.wbpStats is Maybe; players who didn't play (DNP) have Nothing here.
WireBoxStats holds either or both of batting / pitching; a position player has batting but no pitching, a relief pitcher has pitching but no batting (typically), a two-way player has both.
Every batting/pitching field is Maybe Int; absence means 'not reported', forwarded to BattingStats / PitchingStats unchanged.
Fields are NOT validated against each other; e.g. atBats < hits is structurally possible but never seen from MLB.
wbpInningsPitched is Maybe Text on purpose; '6.2' = 20 outs, NOT 6.2 innings.
wbpOuts coexists with wbpInningsPitched; both are Maybe and either could be present alone.

decisions.name: WireTeamMinimalFields
decisions.what: WireTeam parses only id, name, abbreviation, and locationName; ignores division, league, venue, founded year, etc.
why: The DB stores only what we display in lineup/box rendering; ignoring the rest is the simplest way to avoid schema bloat.
If a future feature needs division or league info, we re-parse here without any data migration.
Aeson silently ignores unknown JSON keys, so this is forward-compatible against MLB adding fields.

decisions.name: ModuleLevelFieldNotes
decisions.what: Field-level meaning notes for this wire module
why: WireTeamEnvelope.wireTeams is the only field; envelope wraps the array under the JSON key 'teams'.
WireTeam.wtId is required; the upstream MLB team id used as TeamId in the domain layer.
wtName and wtAbbreviation are required (.:); a team without either is a parse failure.
wtLocationName is optional (.:?) and defaults to T.empty at conversion time.

decisions.name: ModuleLevelFieldNotes
decisions.what: Field-level meaning notes for this wire module (no top-level signatures, only data + FromJSON instances)
why: WirePlayerEnvelope unwraps the top-level 'people' key (NOT 'players' — the MLB endpoint name is misleading).
WirePlayer.wpId is required (.:); always present in real responses.
wpActive is also required; spring training partial records still include this.
Every other field is .:? optional because MLB ships partial records during pre-season.
useName / useLastName are MLB's preferred display names; nameSlug is URL-safe.
WireTeamRef carries id (required) and name (optional); name is decorative, the id is the join key.
WireTeamRef is the embedded team reference inside WirePlayer.wpCurrentTeam, NOT the standalone /teams endpoint shape (WireTeam in Wire.Team).
WirePositionRef has both code ('1','2',...,'10') and abbreviation ('P','C','1B'); convertPosition tries abbreviation first then code.
Both code and abbreviation are Maybe because MLB sometimes ships only one.
WireHandRef is a single-field newtype around a Maybe Text code ('L','R','S'); the wire JSON object also has 'description' but we ignore it.

decisions.name: InlineWireGameTeamParser
decisions.what: WireGameTeam's FromJSON instance manually extracts team.id rather than reusing WireTeamRef from Wire.Player
why: Schedule context only needs the id; pulling in WireTeamRef would either re-export it from Player.hs or duplicate the type.
Inlining the parse keeps the Schedule wire module self-contained.
If schedule entries ever need team names (e.g. for TBD games), this is the place to swap in WireTeamRef.

decisions.name: ModuleLevelFieldNotes
decisions.what: Field-level meaning notes for this wire module
why: WireScheduleEnvelope unwraps the top-level 'dates' array; the envelope's other fields (totalGames, totalEvents, copyright) are ignored.
WireDateEntry.wdeDate is Text in YYYY-MM-DD format, but MLB sometimes drops zero-padding; parseDate in Convert handles both forms.
wdeGames is Maybe [WireGame]; off-days have games absent, NOT empty array (varies by endpoint version).
WireGame.wgGamePk is required; the upstream MLB game id used as GameId in the domain layer.
wgTeams is Maybe; rare partial records (TBD games) lack the teams object entirely.
WireGameTeams.wgtAway / wgtHome are individually Maybe; either side could be missing on TBD opponents (e.g. wildcard placeholder games).
WireGameTeam.wgtTeamId parser drills into the 'team' object then extracts 'id', returning Nothing if either is missing.

decisions.name: TolerantParseStrictRender
decisions.what: parseProviderName returns Maybe rather than failing; renderProviderName is total over the closed sum
why: Reading: an unknown provider name in the database (e.g. an old row from a discontinued provider) shouldn't crash the whole query. The reader can show 'unknown' or skip the row.
Writing: the writer always uses the rendered constant from the sum, so writes are never typos.
Adding a provider is a code change (new constructor + new parse case + new render case); no migration needed because the column is TEXT.

decisions.name: WireFormatNamesAreStable
decisions.what: renderProviderName values ('mlb', 'pelotero-internal') are stable strings that can never change without a data migration
why: The text is stored in DB rows (player_external_id, team_external_id, game_external_id, provider_fetch_log).
Renaming a constructor without renaming the rendered string would silently invalidate every row of that provider.
Test by Show: the constructor name (ProviderMLB) is informational; the wire string ('mlb') is the contract.

renderProviderName: exhaustive over the sum; adding a constructor without a render case is a -Wincomplete-patterns error
produces lowercase, hyphen-separated names matching the SQL convention
parseProviderName: returns Nothing for unknown names rather than failing — see decision TolerantParseStrictRender
case-sensitive: 'MLB' and 'mlb' are distinct, only the second matches
consumed by Pelotero.DB.Rel8Instances DBType ProviderName instance and by Pelotero.DB.FetchLog.fromResult

decisions.name: DefaultsAreLocalDevValues
decisions.what: defaultDBConfig points at localhost:5433 / pelotero-engine with empty user/password
why: These are values for the local Nix dev shell; they fail loudly if used in production (empty user can't auth).
Production setups must set PG* env vars; sops-nix handles this in real deploys.
An alternative was to require all values explicitly, but that breaks 'cabal run' in a dev shell where defaults are convenient.

decisions.name: DbErrorIsOpaqueWrapper
decisions.what: PoolUsageError and MigrationError carry Text rather than the underlying hasql-pool / migration error types
why: Callers shouldn't need to import hasql-pool internals to handle errors; show-of-error is sufficient for logs.
Adding a new error category is a constructor + a renderDBError case.
Cost: structured handling (e.g. distinguishing 'connection refused' from 'syntax error') requires re-parsing the rendered text — acceptable because we don't currently have such a need.

defaultDBConfig: host=localhost, port=5433, db=pelotero-engine, empty user/password, pool=10, timeout=10s
matches Nix dev shell launch script defaults

loadDBConfig.intent: Read DB config from libpq-conventional env vars + two pelotero-specific tunables
notes: PGHOST/PGPORT/PGDATABASE/PGUSER/PGPASSWORD: standard libpq names so external tools (psql, pgbouncer, sops-exec) all set them consistently
PELOTERO_DB_POOL_SIZE / PELOTERO_DB_ACQUIRE_TIMEOUT: app-specific tunables not in libpq's conventions
missing or unparseable env vars fall back to defaultDBConfig field-by-field (no all-or-nothing failure)

poolConfig: private; constructs PoolConfig.Config from a DBConfig
uses staticConnectionSettings (single-host setup) — multi-host failover would require a different builder
realToFrac on the timeout to satisfy hasql-pool's NominalDiffTime parameter
acquire: non-blocking; returns immediately. Pool only opens connections lazily on first runSession.
no validation that the database is reachable until first use
release: drains the pool; safe to call on a partially-used pool
does NOT abort in-flight transactions; finishes them then closes connections
runSession: wraps Pool.use; converts hasql-pool errors to DBError via show
preserves the Right value type a as-is
runTransaction: convenience wrapper: ReadCommitted, Write, single Transaction
atomicity: write commits on success, rolls back on Tx error or thrown exception
isolation level (ReadCommitted) matches PostgreSQL's default; Serializable would be appropriate for cross-row invariants but isn't currently needed
renderDBError: converts to user-facing Text with a category prefix ('DB pool usage error: ', 'Migration error: ')

decisions.name: OwnedMigrationRunner
decisions.what: Custom migration runner instead of hasql-migration
why: hasql-migration is broken against current crypton (which we use for SHA-256) and is effectively unmaintained.
Migrations are a couple hundred lines we can own outright; less cost than maintaining a fork.
Owning the implementation also lets us encode our specific operational policy (immutable migrations, hash mismatch is a hard error) directly.

decisions.name: ImmutableMigrationsHashChecked
decisions.what: Each migration file is hashed (SHA-256) on first apply; subsequent runs verify the hash and abort with Mismatch if the file has changed
why: Prevents accidental edits from silently de-syncing dev/prod schemas.
Forces the convention 'create a new V0042__ file' rather than 'edit V0007__'.
Whitespace-sensitive on purpose: any edit, even cosmetic, trips the alarm. False positives are a feature, not a bug.

decisions.name: PerMigrationTransaction
decisions.what: Each migration runs in its own transaction (not the whole batch)
why: A failure rolls back exactly the offending migration, leaving the prior ones intact.
Avoids the 'partially applied batch' state.
Cost: a migration that includes a CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY (which can't run in a transaction) needs to be split or use a special path. Not yet relevant for this codebase.

decisions.name: FilenameOrderIsApplyOrder
decisions.what: Migration files are sorted lexicographically; apply order = filename order
why: The convention V<NNNN>__<desc>.sql with zero-padded numbers makes lexicographic order match numeric order.
Forgetting to zero-pad (V42__ before V9__) is caught by code review, not by the runner.
An explicit manifest file would be more robust but adds maintenance overhead for marginal benefit.

runMigrations.intent: Apply all .sql files in dir that haven't been applied; verify checksums of those that have
notes: missing directory is a hard error (MigrationError 'Migration directory not found')
SUCCESS path: returns Right MigrationOutcome with totals
MISMATCH path: returns Left MigrationError with the filename
ensures schema_migrations exists via a CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS at the start of applyAll
idempotent: safe to call on every process startup

loadScript: private; reads a file's bytes and computes its SHA-256 hex string
scriptName is the bare filename (Text), not the full path
applyAll: first runs ensureMigrationsTable in its own transaction
then folds over scripts; on the first Mismatch, stops and returns Left
Skipped/Applied counts accumulate in the MigrationOutcome
uses TxS.transaction ReadCommitted Write per migration
applyOne: looks up the prior checksum for this filename; if present and matching, returns Skipped
if present and DIFFERENT, returns Mismatch (does NOT throw — the caller decides)
if absent, runs the SQL via Tx.sql then inserts the (filename, checksum) pair, both in the same transaction so a failure rolls back both
ensureMigrationsTable: CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS schema_migrations (filename TEXT PK, checksum TEXT NOT NULL, applied_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW())
embedded SQL string; cannot be edited without bumping a migration that depends on the table existing
selectChecksum: Statement Text -> Maybe Text; one row or none
uses the prepared-statement cache (True at the end of the Statement constructor)
insertApplied: Statement (Text, Text) -> (); the encoder uses Contravariant fst/snd to project into two separate text params
applied_at fills via the column DEFAULT NOW()
hexSha256: ByteString -> Text; SHA-256 then base16 then UTF-8 decode

decisions.name: OrphanInstancesAreDeliberate
decisions.what: DBType / DBEq / DBOrd instances for domain types live here as orphans; the {-# OPTIONS_GHC -Wno-orphans #-} pragma is intentional
why: Putting them in Pelotero.Domain.Id forces the domain layer to depend on rel8, which is the wrong direction (domain must not know about its persistence library).
Putting them in each Pelotero.DB.* table module produces orphan-conflict warnings as soon as two table modules reference the same domain type.
This module is the lowest place that already imports both the domain types and rel8, so it's the canonical home.
Importers use the empty-import idiom: 'import Pelotero.DB.Rel8Instances ()' to bring instances into scope.

decisions.name: JsonBEncodedForComplexTypes
decisions.what: LeagueScoring, RosterLimits, LineupLimits get DBType via JSONBEncoded deriving via
why: These types are nested records that don't map cleanly to relational columns.
Storing them as JSONB lets the DB index/query them via PostgreSQL's JSONB operators if needed, while keeping the Haskell code working with native records.
Cost: JSON migrations are awkward; if the shape changes, all stored values need an in-place data migration. Acceptable because these change rarely.
Relies on ToJSON / FromJSON instances defined in Pelotero.Domain.Scoring and Pelotero.Domain.Roster.

decisions.name: ProviderNameTextEnumDb
decisions.what: ProviderName decodes via parseTypeInformation, with parseProviderName as the decoder; on unknown values it returns Left, which becomes a hasql query failure
why: Unlike Pelotero.DB.FetchLog.fromResult (which decodes to Maybe and filters), this DBType instance is strict: an unknown provider in the DB is a query failure.

Tables that use ProviderName directly (player_external_id, team_external_id, game_external_id) must only contain known providers, OR the table must decode to Text and convert in code (the FetchLog approach).
This asymmetry is per-table by design: external-id tables are write-controlled; the fetch log is append-only and historical, so it tolerates legacy values.

decisions.name: TwoTablePlayerExternalIdSplit
decisions.what: player table holds the canonical row; player_external_id holds (player_id, provider, external_id) tuples
why: A player can have ids from multiple providers (MLB, internal, future provider X) without schema gymnastics on the player table.
If a player gets re-identified (rare but happens for minor-league call-ups), the player row stays put; only the external_id rows update.
Cost: every upsert is two operations (lookup-or-insert player + insert/skip external id); upsertByExternalIdT encapsulates this.

decisions.name: BatHandStoredAsText
decisions.what: DB column for bat_side / pitch_hand is Text; the API exposes Char
why: PostgreSQL doesn't have a native single-character type smaller than TEXT (CHAR(1) exists but has fixed-length-padding gotchas).
Char in Haskell is multi-byte (Unicode) so storing as Text is structurally correct.
API uses Char because the only legal values are 'L', 'R', 'S' and a Char is the most precise way to encode 'exactly one character of these three'.
charToText / textToChar bridge the two; textToChar uses safeHead so a multi-character value (data corruption) gets truncated rather than crashing.

playerSchema: table 'player' with surrogate id, denormalised name, position, batting/pitching hand as text, active flag, FK to team, last-synced metadata
playerCurrentTeamId is Maybe DbTeamId; a player without a team (free agent, retired) has NULL
playerExternalIdSchema: the natural key is (provider, external_id); not enforced as UNIQUE here but the upsert path relies on it being UNIQUE in practice
charToText: Maybe Char -> Maybe Text via T.singleton; preserves None
textToChar: Maybe Text -> Maybe Char via T.uncons; returns the first char if any, Nothing if empty
if the stored text has more than one character (data corruption), silently truncates to the first — see decision BatHandStoredAsText
fromResult: private; converts the rel8 Player Result row to the public PlayerRow
playerRowId is wrapped in Just because Insert returns DbPlayerId; the inbound row can have Nothing if it's being constructed for insert
insertPlayerT: INSERT ... RETURNING id; uses Abort on conflict (calling on an existing id is a hard error, not silent)
the surrogate id is unsafeDefault (DB-assigned BIGSERIAL); all other fields come from the row
updatePlayerT: WHERE id = pid; updates everything except id
no-op if pid doesn't exist (UPDATE returns 0 rows; we don't check)
getByIdT: single-row select via WHERE; returns the first match or Nothing
if there are duplicates (shouldn't be possible due to PK), takes the first
getAllT: ORDER BY last_name, first_name; returns the entire table
no pagination; fine for ~5000 MLB players
getActiveT: ORDER BY last_name, first_name; WHERE active = TRUE
active is the canonical flag for 'currently rostered'
linkExternalIdT: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING; safe to call repeatedly (e.g. during a re-sync that hits the same provider+external_id)
lookupByExternalIdT: SELECT player_id WHERE provider = ? AND external_id = ?; returns the first match or Nothing
getExternalIdT: reverse lookup: given a DbPlayerId and provider, returns the external_id text
useful for emitting player references back to the upstream provider's namespace

upsertByExternalIdT.intent: Two-step upsert: lookup the player via (provider, external_id); if found, update the player row; if not, insert and link
notes: atomic within a transaction (caller's responsibility to wrap if needed; the pool variant does)

concurrent upserts to the same (provider, external_id) can race: two concurrent inserts would both try linkExternalIdT, the second's DO NOTHING silently ignores — leaving an orphan player. Acceptable because the sync pipeline is single-writer.
returns the resulting DbPlayerId either way

insertPlayer: Pool-flavored wrapper around insertPlayerT in a single transaction
upsertByExternalId: Pool-flavored upsertByExternalIdT, the most common path used by the sync pipeline

decisions.name: MirrorsPlayerSchema
decisions.what: Team table follows the same shape as Player: surrogate id + external_id companion table + same upsertByExternalIdT pattern
why: Conceptual consistency: identical concerns (multi-provider identity, sync metadata) get identical solutions.
Cost: code duplication. A Functor over the table schema would deduplicate this but adds abstraction overhead with little payoff at four tables.
If we add a fifth table with the same pattern, this should be revisited.

teamSchema: table 'team' with surrogate id, name, abbreviation, location_name (city), and last-synced metadata
no FK out — teams are leaves in the FK graph (players and games reference team_id)
teamExternalIdSchema: same shape as player_external_id: (team_id, provider, external_id, fetched_at)
fromResult: teamRowId is Just _teamId (always present after a SELECT)
insertTeamT: INSERT ... RETURNING id; Abort on conflict
all fields except id are from the row; id is unsafeDefault
updateTeamT: WHERE id = tid; updates everything except id
linkExternalIdT: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING; idempotent
lookupByExternalIdT: SELECT team_id WHERE provider AND external_id
getExternalIdT: reverse lookup; given a DbTeamId and provider, returns the upstream external id

notes: lookup via (provider, external_id); if found, update; if not, insert + link
returns DbTeamId either way

upsertByExternalId: Pool-flavored upsertByExternalIdT; consumed by the sync pipeline as the primary write path

decisions.name: GameDateAsDay
decisions.what: game.game_date stores Day (no time of day), not UTCTime
why: Fantasy scoring periods are defined by date in the league's local timezone; game start times within a day are irrelevant for whether the game counts.
Storing as TIMESTAMPTZ would force every query to deal with timezone offset for what is fundamentally a calendar question.
The wire layer parses MLB's full timestamp but the converter discards the time component intentionally.

decisions.name: MirrorsTeamSchema
decisions.what: Same surrogate-id + external_id companion + upsertByExternalIdT pattern as Team and Player
why: See Pelotero.DB.Team.MirrorsPlayerSchema; the rationale extends here. Three tables with this pattern is the threshold where a generic might be worth it; we're at three and not yet refactoring.

gameSchema: table 'game' with surrogate id, game_date (Day), away/home team FKs to team.id, last-synced metadata
gameExternalIdSchema: same shape as player_external_id and team_external_id
getByDateRangeT: WHERE game_date BETWEEN startDay AND endDay (inclusive both ends)
ORDER BY game_date ASC, id ASC for stable cross-day display
consumed by Pelotero.Score.buildPlayerMaps via the Games effect
getByDateRange: Pool-flavored wrapper; inclusive on both ends
insertGameT: INSERT ... RETURNING id; Abort on conflict
updateGameT: WHERE id = gid; updates everything except id
getByDateT: id ordering is stable but not meaningful (insert order); fine for display

upsertByExternalIdT.intent: Same two-step pattern as Team and Player

decisions.name: ProviderColumnIsTextNotEnum
decisions.what: _flProvider is Column f Text, NOT Column f ProviderName
why: The fetch log is append-only and historical; a row written by a provider that no longer exists must remain readable.
If we used the ProviderName DBType (which fails on unknown values), a single legacy row would crash every fetch-log query.
fromResult does the parse and returns Nothing for unparseable rows; getLastFetchT and getRecentFetchesT use mapMaybe to drop them silently from results.
Symmetry with the strict path on player/team/game external_id tables is intentional: those are write-controlled; this one is historical.

decisions.name: RecordCountAsInt32
decisions.what: fetchLogRecordCount is Int32, not Int64 or Int
why: INTEGER (not BIGINT) in PostgreSQL; 2^31 ≈ 2 billion records per fetch is plenty.
Using Int (machine-word) would silently widen on 64-bit platforms, then narrow at the wire boundary — easier to keep it explicit.
An MLB roster fetch yields ~700 records; far from any limit.

fetchLogSchema: table 'provider_fetch_log' with id (BIGSERIAL), provider (TEXT), resource, scope, fetched_at, payload_sha256, record_count (INTEGER)
no PK on (provider, resource, scope) — multiple rows per scope are expected (a 're-fetch' history)
fromResult: Returns Nothing if _flProvider doesn't parse as a known ProviderName — see decision ProviderColumnIsTextNotEnum
fetchLogId and fetchLogFetchedAt are Just because they're set by the DB on insert
recordFetchT: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT Abort; the fetch log is append-only, no upsert semantics
_flId and _flFetchedAt are unsafeDefault (BIGSERIAL and DEFAULT NOW())
getLastFetchT: ORDER BY fetched_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 1; the id-DESC tiebreaker handles same-millisecond fetches
returns the first parseable row from the result via mapMaybe; if the most recent row is from an unknown provider, it's silently skipped
getRecentFetchesT: same ORDER BY pattern, LIMIT lim; returns up to `lim` parseable rows
may return fewer than `lim` if some rows have unknown providers (mapMaybe drop)

decisions.name: ScoringAndLimitsAsJsonbColumns
decisions.what: scoring_config (LeagueScoring), roster_limits (RosterLimits), lineup_limits (LineupLimits) are JSONB columns, not separate tables
why: These types are nested records that don't map cleanly to relational columns.
A separate table per (scoring multiplier per league) would create a 30-row table per league for what is conceptually one record.
Cost: a schema change to the inner records requires a JSONB data migration on every existing row.
Encoded via JSONBEncoded deriving via in Pelotero.DB.Rel8Instances.

decisions.name: StatusAsTextNotEnum
decisions.what: _lcStatus is Column f Text, not the LeagueStatus domain sum
why: Same rationale as ProviderName for the fetch log: tolerate legacy or unrecognised values without crashing reads.
However, the layered domain type LeagueStatus exists as the canonical render/parse pair; this column being Text is the persistence-layer trade-off.
An alternative would be a CHECK constraint enumerating the strings; that's worth doing if status values stabilise.

leagueConfigSchema: table 'league_config' with surrogate id, league_id (Text — user-facing identifier, separate from the surrogate), commissioner, status, JSONB scoring/roster/lineup, draft params, scoring period bounds
insertLeagueConfigT: INSERT ... RETURNING id; Abort on conflict
JSONB columns serialize via the JSONBEncoded DBType instance
updateLeagueConfigT: WHERE id = lcid; updates everything except id
getByLeagueIdT: league_id should be UNIQUE in practice; not enforced at the schema level here
getAllT: fine for tens to hundreds of leagues

decisions.name: TeamKeySeparateFromName
decisions.what: league_team has both team_key (stable identifier within a league) and name (mutable display name)
why: Owners change team names mid-season; references from elsewhere (rosters, draft picks) must remain stable.
team_key is the join key; name is the rendered string.
(league_config_id, team_key) is the natural compound key; lookupByKeyT relies on it being UNIQUE in practice.

leagueTeamSchema: table 'league_team' with surrogate id, FK to league_config, team_key (stable), name, owner
no last-synced metadata — league teams are user-managed, not externally synced
insertLeagueTeamT: INSERT ... RETURNING id; Abort on conflict
updateLeagueTeamT: WHERE id = ltid; updates everything except id
team_key is mutable here; in practice changing it breaks downstream rosters via FK constraints
lookupByKeyT: WHERE league_config_id AND team_key; returns the first match or Nothing
the (league_config_id, team_key) UNIQUE invariant is implicit, not enforced here
getForLeagueT: ORDER BY name; all teams in a league
name-order is stable enough for display but not for joins
deleteT: DELETE WHERE id; cascading deletes on dependent rows (rosters, lineups, picks) are handled by FK ON DELETE in the schema

decisions.name: UpsertOnPlayerNotSlot
decisions.what: addSlotT does ON CONFLICT (league_team_id, player_id) DO UPDATE SET slot, NOT (league_team_id, slot)
why: The natural-feeling 'a slot can hold one player' is wrong for fantasy; multiple OF/UTIL slots per team is normal.
The actual invariant is 'a player is in at most one slot per team'.
Adding a player who's already on the roster moves them to the new slot rather than failing or duplicating.
This matches the legacy hasql module's semantics, preserving a UI behaviour that owners depend on.

decisions.name: SurrogateIdAndCreatedAtHidden
decisions.what: The public RosterSlotRow type omits surrogate id and created_at; the rel8 schema includes them
why: rel8's TableSchema needs to know about every column to do SELECT *.
The public API doesn't need them — id is BIGSERIAL, created_at is server-managed.
Hiding them keeps callers from accidentally relying on ordering by created_at or constructing rows with synthetic ids.

rosterSlotSchema: table 'roster_slot' with surrogate id, FK to league_team, slot (Text), FK to player, created_at
fromResult: private; drops the hidden surrogate id and created_at
this is why RosterSlotRow has fewer fields than the rel8 RosterSlotE shape
addSlotT: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (league_team_id, player_id) DO UPDATE SET slot
Upsert.set preserves id, league_team_id, player_id, created_at from old; only slot updates
updateWhere = lit True (always update on conflict — see decision UpsertOnPlayerNotSlot)
getSlotsForTeamT: WHERE league_team_id; ORDER BY slot, player_id
slot ordering is alphabetical Text; player_id ordering as a tiebreaker for stable display
removeSlotT: removes from any slot — the player is uniquely identified by league_team + player_id (not slot)
removePlayerFromTeamT: kept for API readability where the caller's intent is 'remove from team' vs. 'remove from this slot specifically'
replaceTeamRosterT: transaction-internal sequence: clearTeamRosterT then mapM_ addSlotT
entirely within the caller's transaction; either everything replaces or nothing does
concurrent calls would race on the same team — caller's responsibility to serialise
countBySlotT: COUNT(*) WHERE league_team_id AND slot; used for limit-checking before adds
returns 0 on empty (countStar returns a singleton list with 0)

decisions.name: MirrorsRosterSlotExactly
decisions.what: lineup_slot is structurally identical to roster_slot: same shape, same upsert semantics, same hidden id/created_at
why: Lineups and rosters are different concepts (lineup = today's actives, roster = entire owned set) but the storage shape is identical.
Keeping them as parallel modules with parallel schemas avoids prematurely abstracting and lets us evolve them independently if/when they diverge.
Cost: code duplication (two near-identical modules).

lineupSlotSchema: table 'lineup_slot' with surrogate id, FK to league_team, slot (Text), FK to player, created_at
fromResult: private; same omission of id and created_at as RosterSlot.fromResult
addSlotT: same upsert pattern as RosterSlot.addSlotT: ON CONFLICT (league_team_id, player_id) DO UPDATE SET slot
moves a player to a new lineup slot rather than failing
getSlotsForTeamT: WHERE league_team_id; ORDER BY slot, player_id

decisions.name: NoSurrogateIdNaturalKey
decisions.what: player_ranking has no surrogate id; (league_team_id, player_id) is the primary key
why: Unlike roster_slot/lineup_slot where the (team, player) pair has a 'context' (the slot string), a ranking pair carries only its rank_slot integer.
There's no scenario where a team has two ranking entries for the same player.
Fewer columns, simpler schema.

decisions.name: AbortOnConflictForRankings
decisions.what: insertOneT uses Abort, not Upsert; replaceRankingsT works by clear-then-fill
why: Rankings are typically replaced wholesale (re-rank the entire pool) rather than tweaked incrementally.
Abort + clear-then-fill is conceptually simpler than upsert and avoids the 'updateWhere lit True' boilerplate.
Cost: one DELETE + N INSERTs vs. one INSERT ON CONFLICT per row. For ~100-row rankings, irrelevant.

playerRankingSchema: table 'player_ranking' with FK to league_team, FK to player, rank_slot (Int32), updated_at
PK is (league_team_id, player_id) — no surrogate id
fromResult: private; rel8 Result -> PlayerRankingRow; drops updated_at
insertOneT: concurrent inserts of the same (league_team, player) fail loudly; the replace path's clearRankingsT first avoids this
getRankingsForTeamT: rank_slot ordering puts higher-preference players first (assuming caller follows the convention rank=1 means top pick)

decisions.name: AppendOnlyDraftPicks
decisions.what: Only insert (recordPick) and read (getPicksForLeague, getPickCount) operations exist; no update or delete
why: Picks are historical events; once made, they don't get edited or undone.
If a wrong pick needs correction, the convention is to insert a new pick at the next pick_number rather than mutating the prior row.
Audit trail integrity: a query at any point in time gives the actual sequence of picks made.

draftPickSchema: table 'draft_pick' with surrogate id, FK to league_config, pick_number (Int32 — 1-indexed), FK to league_team, FK to player, picked_at
fromResult: wraps id and picked_at in Just (always present after SELECT)
recordPickT: INSERT ... RETURNING id; Abort on conflict
_dpId and _dpPickedAt are unsafeDefault (BIGSERIAL and DEFAULT NOW())
getPicksForLeagueT: pick_number ordering recovers the actual draft sequence
getPickCountT: used to figure out 'whose pick is next?' as count + 1

decisions.name: TwoTablesNotOne
decisions.what: Batting and pitching are separate tables (game_player_batting and game_player_pitching), not one wide table
why: Batting has ~25 stat columns, pitching has ~40. Combining gives a 65-column row that's mostly NULL for any given player.
Querying 'all batting lines this week' becomes a clean SELECT from one table without WHERE filtering on column NULLness.
A two-way player (pitcher who bats) gets two rows, one per table — correct because both stat lines are independently meaningful.

decisions.name: InningsPitchedAsOuts
decisions.what: The pitching table stores INTEGER outs (multiples of 1/3 inning), NOT the wire string '6.2'
why: The wire-format string is a known footgun (see Pelotero.MLB.Wire.Boxscore decision InningsPitchedAsText).
Storing as outs makes SUM, AVG, and arithmetic exact; a decimal column would lose precision.
Conversion happens at write time; readers always see exact integer outs.

decisions.name: UpdatedAtFromSqlNow
decisions.what: Upsert sets updated_at = RT.now (a SQL-side NOW()), preserving created_at from the existing row
why: RT.now is rel8's Expr-level NOW() — runs at DB transaction time, not at Haskell wall-clock time.
The pattern is: created_at fixed at first insert, updated_at refreshed on every upsert.
Taking the timestamp client-side and passing it via R.lit would risk skew between client and DB clocks.

battingSchema: table 'game_player_batting' with FK to game, FK to player, FK to team (nullable), 25 stat columns (all Maybe Int32), created_at, updated_at
natural PK: (game_id, player_id) — same player twice in the same game is impossible per MLB
pitchingSchema: table 'game_player_pitching' with FK to game, FK to player, FK to team (nullable), 40+ stat columns, innings_pitched_outs as Int32, created_at, updated_at
fromBattingResult: private; rel8 BattingE Result -> BattingRow; drops created_at and updated_at
fromPitchingResult: private; rel8 PitchingE Result -> PitchingRow; drops created_at and updated_at
battingRowToExpr: private; BattingRow -> BattingE Expr for use in INSERT VALUES clause
created_at and updated_at are unsafeDefault — DB sets them on insert
upsertBattingT: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (game_id, player_id) DO UPDATE
set: keeps id-like columns from old, takes stats from new, preserves created_at, sets updated_at = NOW()
updateWhere = lit True (always update on conflict)
deleteBattingForGameT: useful when re-ingesting a corrected boxscore: delete then re-upsert

decisions.name: OneOperationOneTransaction
decisions.what: Database has a single operation, runTx, which acquires a connection and runs the transaction in isolation
why: Each runTx is its own atomic unit; no need for callers to manage connection scope.
Trade-off: composing multiple runTx calls is NOT one transaction — they're independent. If you need a multi-step atomic operation, build a single Transaction and pass it to one runTx.
This matches Pool.runTransaction's contract; the Database effect is a thin wrapper to make it dispatchable through the effectful machinery.

decisions.name: DbErrorBecomesIoError
decisions.what: runOrThrow converts Either DBError to IO via ioError when the result is Left
why: The effect interface is total (returns a, not Either DBError a) so callers don't have to plumb error handling through every Database call.
DB errors at the effect layer are exceptional, not expected; treating them as IO exceptions is consistent with how unexpected DB failures behave in mainstream Haskell.
userError gives a structured message but loses the DBError constructor — fine for logs, lossy for programmatic handling. If we needed structured handling, we'd wrap in a custom exception type.

runTx: the only public operation; takes a Tx.Transaction a and returns Eff es a
each call is one independent transaction; no nesting, no batching
writes commit on success, roll back on exception

runDatabasePool.intent: Production interpreter: runs each runTx via Pool.runTransaction and unwraps the DBError
notes: throws userError on Left DBError; never returns Left to the caller
rationale for throwing rather than wrapping in a custom error monad is captured in DbErrorBecomesIoError

runOrThrow: private; lifts IO (Either DBError a) to Eff es a, throwing userError on Left
show-of-DBError loses structure but preserves the rendered category prefix from renderDBError

decisions.name: FixedTimeForTests
decisions.what: runClockFixed is the test interpreter; every now call returns the same fixed UTCTime
why: Sync code uses Clock.now to stamp synced_at on rows; tests need the same value to compare against.
An incrementing-on-each-call interpreter would test more edge cases but adds complexity.
If a test needs different timestamps across calls, it can stack multiple Clock interpreters (run a fixed time, perform some work, swap interpreters).

now: the only operation; returns the current time per the active interpreter
runClockIO: IO interpreter; calls Data.Time.getCurrentTime per call
runClockFixed: fixed-time interpreter; every call returns the same UTCTime

decisions.name: TwoInterpretersHttpAndFixture
decisions.what: MLBClient has runMLBClientHTTP (production) and runMLBClientFixture (offline tests reading JSON files from disk)
why: The fixture interpreter exercises the same wire-to-domain conversion path (Pelotero.MLB.Convert) as production, just with file reads instead of HTTP.
Fixture tests don't depend on network, MLB API uptime, or rate limits.
The fixture path manually computes the SHA over teams+players bytes (same order as fetchRosters), so test-mode SHAs match production semantics.

decisions.name: FixtureBoxscoresOverride
decisions.what: MLBFixture has fixtureBoxscores :: Map Int FilePath for per-game path overrides, falling back to fixturesDir/boxscore-<gamePk>.json
why: Most tests use the conventional path; the override exists for tests that need to point a specific gamePk at a corrupted/edge-case fixture file.
Map.findWithDefault is the right primitive — common case is one path-pattern, edge case is per-id.
Avoids forcing every test to lay out its own complete fixture directory.

decisions.name: WireToDomainTeamCopiedFromFetch
decisions.what: runMLBClientFixture inlines its own copy of wireToDomainTeam rather than importing from Pelotero.MLB.Fetch
why: wireToDomainTeam is private to Fetch; exporting it for one test caller felt heavier than four lines of duplication.
If a third caller appears, this should move to a shared Convert helper.
See Pelotero.MLB.Fetch decision WireToDomainTeamPrivate for the symmetric reasoning.

fetchRosters: returns the same Either String FetchedRosters as Pelotero.MLB.Fetch.fetchRosters
fetchBoxscoreRaw: MLBClient send-only API for boxscore raw bytes

runMLBClientHTTP.intent: Production interpreter; delegates each operation to Pelotero.MLB.Fetch via liftIO
notes: no caching, no retries, no rate limiting at this layer

defaultFixture: constructs an MLBFixture with empty fixtureBoxscores; all boxscore paths default to the conventional layout

runMLBClientFixture.intent: Test interpreter; reads fixture files from disk and runs them through the same Convert pipeline as production
notes: FetchRosters: reads teams-<season>.json and players-<season>.json from fixturesDir, parses both, computes SHA over their concatenation (same order as production fetch)
FetchSchedule: reads schedule-<startDate>-<endDate>.json from fixturesDir
FetchBoxscoreRaw: looks up the gamePk in fixtureBoxscores; falls back to fixturesDir/boxscore-<gamePk>.json
missing files become Left with a path-prefixed error, matching production error shape

decisions.name: InMemoryFetchLogIsList
decisions.what: runFetchLogInMemory uses an IORef [FetchLogRow] (cons-prepended), not a Map
why: Tests typically write a few rows and read the most recent; a list is fine.
Cons-prepending makes 'most recent first' free — getLastFetch's filter then takes head.
If a test needs to assert a specific fetch order (insertion order forward), the Map alternative would force a separate counter.

recordFetch: FetchLog send-only; records a new fetch row
getLastFetch: FetchLog send-only; given (provider, resource, scope), returns the most recent fetch or Nothing
runFetchLogDB: GetLastFetch via getLastFetchT (already does ORDER BY fetched_at DESC LIMIT 1 in SQL)
runFetchLogInMemory: IO-backed test interpreter using an IORef [FetchLogRow]
GetLastFetch filters by exact provider/resource/scope match and returns the head (most recent due to cons-prepend)
matching predicate: provider AND resource AND scope all equal — note the AND, NOT a partial match

decisions.name: InMemoryAssignsAutoIncrementId
decisions.what: runPlayersInMemory's UpsertPlayerByExternalId uses an internal nextId counter (Int starting at 1), wrapping in DbPlayerId
why: Mirrors the DB's BIGSERIAL behaviour without needing an actual sequence.
Counter is per-IORef (per-runner-instance), so two concurrent test runs don't share ids — each test gets a fresh PlayerStore.
The id only matters for joins within the same test; production semantics aren't tested here.

upsertPlayerByExternalId: Players send-only; same semantics as DB upsertByExternalId
getActivePlayers: Players send-only; all players where active=True
emptyStore: private; PlayerStore Map.empty Map.empty 1 (note: nextId starts at 1, NOT 0)
runPlayersInMemory: UpsertPlayerByExternalId: if (provider, externalId) found, update rowsByDb keeping the existing id; else assign nextId and insert into both maps
atomicModifyIORef ensures concurrent calls within one test don't corrupt the store
GetActivePlayers iterates all rows and filters by playerRowActive — no index, O(n)

decisions.name: MirrorsPlayersInMemoryShape
decisions.what: TeamStore has the same external-id-map + db-rows-map + nextId-counter shape as PlayerStore
why: Same trade-offs as Players: per-runner counter mimicking BIGSERIAL, no FK enforcement.
Code duplication is acceptable at two test interpreters; would be reconsidered at four.

runTeamsInMemory: IORef-based test interpreter; same upsert/lookup/get semantics as runPlayersInMemory
GetAllTeams returns Map.toList values; order is Map's internal Ord on DbTeamId

decisions.name: GameStoreHasReverseLookupMap
decisions.what: The in-memory game store maintains both an external-id->db-id map AND a db-id->external-id map
why: GetGameExternalId requires reverse lookup; iterating the forward map with elem-on-value would be O(n) per call.
Two maps cost twice the memory but make every lookup O(log n).
The pattern isn't repeated in Players/Teams because GetPlayerExternalId / GetTeamExternalId aren't part of those effects (those effects don't surface reverse lookup at the moment).

getGamesByDateRange: Games send-only; range listing inclusive on both ends
consumed by Pelotero.Score.buildPlayerMaps to enumerate games in a scoring period
emptyGameStore: three maps because of the reverse-lookup decision
runGamesInMemory: UpsertGameByExternalId maintains both forward and reverse maps consistently
GetGamesByDate iterates all rows and filters by gameRowGameDate — O(n)
GetGamesByDateRange iterates all rows and filters with two predicates — O(n)

runLeagueConfigDB: no in-memory interpreter — league configs are heavyweight (JSONB-encoded scoring/limits) and tests for league config logic prefer round-tripping through the actual DB or constructing rows directly

runLeagueTeamDB: no in-memory interpreter; league teams are tested through the DB layer or directly via repository functions

runRosterSlotDB: no in-memory interpreter; roster manipulation logic is tested via the DB layer

runLineupSlotDB: no in-memory interpreter; mirrors RosterSlot in this respect

runDraftPickDB: no in-memory interpreter — draft picks are append-only and the in-memory equivalent would be a list, identical to FetchLog's pattern

decisions.name: UpstreamAndSurrogateAreDistinctTypes
decisions.what: PlayerId / TeamId / GameId (upstream MLB ids) and DbPlayerId / DbTeamId / DbGameId (surrogate DB BIGSERIAL ids) are different newtypes
why: Conflating them led to bugs: a function expecting an MLB id received a DB surrogate, the SQL succeeded with the wrong row, and nothing complained.
Newtype distinctness forces the conversion to be explicit (a lookup against player_external_id) rather than a coerce.
The cost is more wrappers; the win is the type system catching crossings of the layer boundary.

decisions.name: TextIdsForUserSpaces
decisions.what: LeagueId and FantasyTeamId wrap Text, not Int
why: Leagues and fantasy teams have user-chosen identifiers (e.g. 'east-coast-2025', 'rocketeers'), not auto-incremented numbers.
Storing them as Text keeps the surface API matching how owners refer to their teams.
Database surrogate keys (DbLeagueConfigId, DbLeagueTeamId) are still Int64 for indexing efficiency; user-facing stays Text.

decisions.name: NoSmartConstructorsHere
decisions.what: All newtypes have public constructors and accessors; no smart-constructor validation
why: Validation (rejecting nonsense like PlayerId 0) happens at the wire boundary in Pelotero.MLB.Convert.convertPlayer.
Forcing a smart constructor here means every test has to import it instead of just typing PlayerId 1.
The wire layer is the single source of truth for what counts as a valid id; this module is structural only.

decisions.name: ModuleStructureNotes
decisions.what: What this module exports (chase has no signatures here, only newtypes)
why: MLB identifiers (Int-wrapped): PlayerId, TeamId, GameId, SeasonYear.
Fantasy identifiers (Text-wrapped): LeagueId, FantasyTeamId.
Draft identifiers (Int-wrapped): DraftPickNumber (1-indexed pick ordinal), RankSlot (preference order within a team's ranking).
Database surrogate identifiers (Int64-wrapped, BIGSERIAL): DbPlayerId, DbTeamId, DbGameId, DbLeagueConfigId, DbLeagueTeamId, DbDraftPickId.
All newtypes derive Show, Eq, Ord stock; no other instances at this layer (rel8 instances live in Pelotero.DB.Rel8Instances).

decisions.name: ExhaustiveSumNoCatchAll
decisions.what: The Position type is an exhaustive sum of MLB's ten positions; parsePosition returns Nothing on anything else
why: Positions are a small, stable set defined by MLB rules.
An 'Other Text' fallback constructor would make the type infectious — every consumer would have to handle 'this might be a string'.
Errors at the wire boundary surface as warnings, not silent fallbacks.

decisions.name: TwoWayPlayerNotModelled
decisions.what: MLB's 'TWP' (two-way player, e.g. Ohtani) is intentionally not parsed
why: TWP requires a richer domain model (a player has multiple primary positions with separate stat lines).
